solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Run around quickly in small sort of van (7)

blocks.note: S = small, as on clothing labels
a camper is a van fitted out for living in

annotation.surface: Someone dashing about in a cramped little camper van.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Run around quickly in' reads as one phrase, but 'in' only joins the definition to the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: To scamper is to run about quickly and lightly, like a child or a small animal.

entries.clue: Boxer possibly trained to do this sort of bicycle (3,2,3,3)

annotation.definition: Boxer possibly trained to do this

blocks.clueFragment: Boxer possibly trained to do this
blocks.note: a boxer is a breed of dog; this is a begging trick, rearing back on the haunches with front paws raised
an old-fashioned upright bicycle whose rider sits bolt upright, like a begging dog

annotation.surface: A boxer in training on an exercise bike.
annotation.walkthrough: The boxer is a dog, not a fighter. A sit-up-and-beg bicycle is the traditional British upright bike with high handlebars.
annotation.definitionFit: Both the dog trick and the upright bicycle are called sit up and beg.

entries.clue: Not many misused “bad” for “good”, for example (7)

indicatorNotes.misused: the letters are used wrongly, put into the wrong order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A grumble that few people misuse slang like 'bad' meaning 'good'.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests slang where 'bad' means 'good'; the definition just wants a word of opposite meaning.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Bad' is the opposite of 'good', so it is an example of an antonym.

entries.clue: Quietly show excitement about old luxury flat (9)

indicatorNotes.about: ENTHUSE goes about, around, the O

blocks.note: p = piano, quietly in music
to enthuse is to show excitement
O = old

annotation.surface: Someone trying not to gush too loudly over a grand old apartment.
annotation.walkthrough: P for quietly comes from musical notation (piano). 'Quietly show excitement' reads as one restrained reaction, but 'Quietly' is a separate piece.
annotation.definitionFit: A penthouse is a luxurious flat on the top floor of a building.

entries.clue: Live on edge (6)

blocks.note: re = on, concerning
a side is an edge

annotation.surface: Living with your nerves permanently frayed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On edge' looks like one phrase meaning nervous; split it into two words for the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to live somewhere and to have your home there mean the same.

entries.clue: An exam to treat with contempt? (4)

blocks.note: a practice exam sat before the real one
to ridicule or scoff at

annotation.surface: A student scornfully dismissing an exam.
annotation.walkthrough: In British schools a mock is a practice exam sat before the real one.
annotation.definitionFit: Mock is both a trial exam and a verb meaning to ridicule.

entries.clue: Samoans corralling flightless bird (3)

indicatorNotes.corralling: the word pens the answer inside itself

blocks.note: the letters sit in the middle of the word, after SA and before NS

annotation.surface: Pacific islanders rounding up a large bird.
annotation.walkthrough: The moa was a giant flightless bird of New Zealand, now extinct.
annotation.definitionFit: The moa was a huge bird that could not fly.

entries.clue: In deep sleep, minute butterfly (5)

indicatorNotes.In: 'In' says the next piece sits inside the sleep word

blocks.note: a coma is a deep unconsciousness
m = minute

annotation.surface: A tiny butterfly fast asleep.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Minute' looks like 'tiny' describing the butterfly; it is the abbreviation for a unit of time.
annotation.definitionFit: The comma is a British butterfly named for a white comma-shaped mark on its wing.

entries.clue: Giant bird with a name (5)

blocks.note: a tit is a small songbird
used as is
n = name

annotation.surface: A huge bird that has been given a name.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Giant bird' looks like one phrase for an ostrich or moa; 'Giant' alone is the definition, and the bird is a tiny one.
annotation.definitionFit: A titan is a giant, after the Titans of Greek myth.

entries.clue: What insects may have done as south got hotter (7)

blocks.note: S = south
to warm is to get hotter

annotation.surface: Bugs gathering as the southern weather heated up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'As' only joins the definition to the wordplay; the definition is a description rather than a synonym.
annotation.definitionFit: Bees and other insects swarm when they gather in a dense moving mass.

entries.clue: Never fear a battleship (11)

blocks.note: to dread is to fear
nought = nothing, not at all, as in 'never'

annotation.surface: A slogan of courage, then a warship.
annotation.walkthrough: The ship's name literally means 'fear nothing', which 'Never fear' paraphrases; the two halves are read in reverse order.
annotation.definitionFit: HMS Dreadnought gave her name to a whole class of big-gun battleships.

entries.clue: Run smartly back for tack (3)

indicatorNotes.back: 'back' says go back the way you came, reading the letters right to left

blocks.note: to nip is to go somewhere quickly, as in 'nip to the shops'

annotation.surface: A sailor told to hurry back and change tack.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tack' looks nautical; it is the small nail, which a pin can stand for.
annotation.definitionFit: A tack is a short pin or nail used to fasten things.

entries.clue: Commissioned exactly what’s required and was sure of success (3,2,4)

blocks.note: got something made to order, read literally word by word
idiom: to have it made is to be certain of success

annotation.surface: A client orders a bespoke item and feels their success is guaranteed.
annotation.walkthrough: The first half is the literal reading of the phrase, the second its idiomatic one.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone who had it made was set up to succeed without difficulty.

entries.clue: Ordinary people, those fools (3,6)

blocks.note: them = those, as in 'them apples'
an ass is a fool

annotation.surface: A snob dismissing ordinary people as idiots.
annotation.walkthrough: The break falls differently in wordplay and answer: THEM + ASSES regroups as THE MASSES.
annotation.definitionFit: A fixed phrase for the general public, as opposed to an elite.

entries.clue: Students receiving substantial amount of storage in the cloud (6)

indicatorNotes.receiving: whatever is receiving something takes it in, so the students hold the storage inside them

blocks.note: NUS = National Union of Students
1MB, one megabyte, with the 1 read as I

annotation.surface: Students getting plenty of cloud storage for their files.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Storage in the cloud' reads as online computing; the cloud is the definition. NUS is the UK's National Union of Students.
annotation.definitionFit: A meteorological term for a dark grey rain-bearing cloud.

entries.clue: Came across bricklayer’s tool and how to use it? (6)

blocks.note: to come across someone is to meet them
a hod is an open box on a pole for carrying bricks

annotation.surface: Finding a hod and wondering how to use it.
annotation.walkthrough: The 'it' in the definition points back to the hod, so the clue hangs together as one scene.
annotation.definitionFit: A way or procedure for doing something, so it tells you how to use the tool.

entries.clue: Emergency resource in hotel is out of order (7)

indicatorNotes.is out of order: the letters are not in their proper order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: The hotel's emergency phone is broken.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container instruction; it is part of the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A hotline is a direct phone line for emergencies or urgent help.

entries.clue: Prejudiced bishop cast aside (6)

indicatorNotes.cast: the letters are thrown, cast about, into a new order

blocks.note: B = bishop, as in chess notation
ASIDE with its letters rearranged

annotation.surface: A prejudiced bishop being thrown out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cast aside' looks like one phrase meaning rejected; 'cast' is the anagram signal working on 'aside'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean leaning unfairly for or against someone.

entries.clue: Book all-Ireland ace dancer (9)

blocks.note: b = book
used as is
Erin is a poetic name for Ireland
A = ace, on playing cards

annotation.surface: Booking a star dancer for an all-Ireland competition.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Book' looks like a verb, to hire; it is only B.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: she is a female ballet dancer.

entries.clue: Contract to rent meadows with house at the rear (5)

indicatorNotes.at the rear: take the letter at the back of 'house'

blocks.note: a lea is a meadow
last letter of hous(E)

annotation.surface: Renting some fields with a house behind them.
annotation.walkthrough: 'House at the rear' reads as a building behind the fields; only the last letter of 'house' is used.
annotation.definitionFit: A lease is a contract letting someone rent property.

entries.clue: Number required to constitute company? (3)

blocks.note: reads like a legal minimum of members for forming something
the surface pushes a business firm; the setter means company as in having someone with you, as in the proverb about a crowd

annotation.surface: A question about the minimum number of people needed to form a business.
annotation.walkthrough: The proverb 'two's company, three's a crowd' supplies the number; the question mark flags the shift from business to friendship.
annotation.definitionFit: The proverb says two's company, so two people is the number needed.

entries.clue: Girls following grand spectacles (7)

indicatorNotes.following: 'following' means coming after, so the girls are placed after G

blocks.note: G = grand, a thousand pounds
lasses = girls

annotation.surface: Girls trailing behind a grand show.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spectacles' looks like grand shows; here they are eyeglasses.
annotation.definitionFit: Spectacles and glasses are both lenses worn to correct vision.

entries.clue: Cat shortly coming up to drink (3)

indicatorNotes.shortly: the word is cut short, losing its last letter
indicatorNotes.coming up: in a down entry, the letters read upwards

blocks.note: PUSS, a cat, loses its last letter

annotation.surface: A cat soon to come up and lap at a drink.
annotation.walkthrough: PUSS is a familiar word for a cat; in a down clue 'coming up' turns the shortened word upside down.
annotation.definitionFit: To sup is to drink, taking small mouthfuls.

entries.clue: Undercover police operation hurt a little (5)

blocks.note: a trap in which police pose as criminals
cause a sharp but brief pain

annotation.surface: A police raid in which someone got slightly injured.
annotation.walkthrough: Two unrelated meanings sit side by side; the police sense comes from con-artist slang.
annotation.definitionFit: Sting names both a police trap and a brief sharp pain.

entries.clue: Carry on, but glance back (4)

indicatorNotes.back: 'back' says go back the way you came, reading the letters right to left

blocks.note: a peek is a quick glance

annotation.surface: Advice to keep walking but look over your shoulder.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Glance back' reads as looking behind you; it signals PEEK read the other way.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of continue, as in keeping going.

entries.clue: Remove perfume? That’s a comedown (7)

blocks.note: the prefix de- means to remove, as in de-ice
scent = perfume

annotation.surface: Someone stripped of their perfume, finding it a letdown.
annotation.walkthrough: DE-SCENT would mean to remove the scent, which the question mark flags as a playful coinage.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a fall in status is both a going down and a comedown.
